title: How can trade turn into forced control?
essentialQuestion: How did a company's wish to control the nutmeg trade change life on the Banda Islands, and whose voices are missing from its records?
learningGoal: Explain how the VOC's monopoly turned trade on the Banda Islands into forced control, and say what a company painting can and cannot show.

warmUp.question: What changes for a seller who is allowed only one buyer?
options: They can choose the best price
They lose their choice of buyer

evidence.question: Which source was made in 1621, and which was made more than 40 years later? Who made each one?

cards.title: Two real sources about Banda, both made for the VOC

sources.caption: Source 1: A report by Jan Pieterszoon Coen, 6 May 1621 (Dutch National Archives)
details: Written by Coen, the VOC leader who led the attack on Banda in 1621.
It reports the company's own decisions during the attack on Banda Besar, the largest island.
It is a company record made at the time, kept today in the VOC's archive in The Hague.
Limit: Coen led the attack and wanted to defend it. In his letters he claimed almost nobody escaped, which was not true.
Limit: the archives say their records hold no Bandanese voices. This source tells the story from the company's side only.

sources.caption: Source 2: A painting of Banda Neira, about 1662–63 (Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam)
details: The VOC's office in Amsterdam paid the workshop of the painter Johannes Vingboons to make it.
It shows the island from above: forts, a Dutch ship, a village and neat rows of nutmeg trees.
The museum says the painters worked from company maps, and some parts, like the hills at the back, were imagined.
Limit: it was made more than 40 years after 1621, far away, for the company. It shows no Bandanese person's experience.

events.text: Portuguese traders reach Banda and buy spices, as many traders before them did.
The first Dutch ships reach Banda. They pay port fees and buy nutmeg and mace.
A VOC fleet comes to Banda Neira and starts to build a fort. Years of fighting follow.
A VOC force led by Coen attacks. Many Bandanese people are killed, enslaved or forced to leave.
Coen writes a report about the company's decisions on Banda (Source 1).
A painters' workshop in the Netherlands paints Banda Neira for the VOC (Source 2).

sections.heading: Nutmeg and many traders
sections.text: The Banda Islands are small islands in eastern Indonesia. For hundreds of years, they were the only place in the world where nutmeg trees grew. The tree's seed gives nutmeg, and the red skin around the seed gives a spice called mace. Buyers far away paid a lot for both. Traders came from Indonesia, China, India, Persia and Arabia. Later, ships came from Portugal, the Netherlands and England. Bandanese leaders were skilled traders, and they chose whom to sell to. Selling spice also paid for food, because the islands grew very little.
sections.simpler: The Banda Islands are in Indonesia. For a long time, only Banda had nutmeg trees. Nutmeg is a spice from the seed. Mace is a spice from the red skin on the seed. People far away paid a lot for them. Traders came from many places in Asia, and later from Europe. Banda's leaders were good traders. They chose who to sell to.

sections.heading: The VOC wants a monopoly
sections.text: The Dutch East India Company, called the VOC, wanted a monopoly. It wanted to be the only buyer of Banda's nutmeg, so no one else could compete. In 1609, a VOC fleet came to Banda Neira, one of the islands, and began to build a fort. The people there refused the company's demands, and years of fighting followed. In 1621, a VOC force led by Jan Pieterszoon Coen attacked the islands. Many Bandanese people were killed. Others were enslaved or forced to leave. Some escaped to other islands, where people kept Banda's history alive in songs and dances. After 1621, the VOC gave the land to settlers, and enslaved people were forced to grow the nutmeg.
sections.simpler: A Dutch company called the VOC came to Banda. It wanted a monopoly. It wanted to be the only buyer of nutmeg. In 1609, it began to build a fort. The people of Banda said no. They fought for years. In 1621, the VOC attacked again. Many Bandanese people were killed. Others were made slaves or forced to leave. Some escaped to other islands. They kept Banda's history alive in songs and dances. Then enslaved people had to grow the nutmeg.

sections.heading: A company picture, made later
sections.text: The second picture is a painting of Banda Neira from about 1662, more than 40 years after the attack. The VOC paid a painters' workshop in the Netherlands to make it. It shows forts, a ship, houses and neat rows of nutmeg trees. It does not show the people who were harmed, or the people who worked in those gardens. The painting shows the company's perspective. Coen's own reports from 1621 are company sources too. In his letters, he wrote that almost nobody escaped, but that was not true. So historians compare sources, and they also listen to the songs and stories that Bandanese people passed down.
sections.simpler: The second picture is a painting. It was made about 40 years after the attack. The VOC paid for it. It shows a fort, a ship and nutmeg trees. It does not show the people who were hurt. It shows the company's perspective. Coen wrote reports too. He said almost nobody escaped. That was not true. So historians check many sources. They also listen to Bandanese songs and stories.

glossary.definition: A spice made from the seed of a tree.
glossary.example: For hundreds of years, nutmeg trees grew only on the Banda Islands.

glossary.definition: A Dutch trading company that also used soldiers and ruled land.
glossary.example: The VOC wanted to be the only buyer of Banda's nutmeg.

glossary.definition: When one group controls selling or buying, and shuts others out.
glossary.example: With a monopoly, the VOC would be the only buyer of nutmeg.

glossary.definition: How the maker of a source sees and shows events.
glossary.example: The painting shows the company's perspective, not the Bandanese one.

checks.question: What did the VOC want when it tried to get a monopoly?

options.text: To share Banda's nutmeg with all traders
options.feedback: Not quite. A monopoly shuts other traders out. Read the start of the second part again.

options.text: To be the only buyer of Banda's nutmeg
options.feedback: Yes. A monopoly means one group controls the trade, so no one else can compete.

options.text: To help Banda grow more of its own food
options.feedback: Not quite. The VOC wanted control of the spice trade. Read the second part again.

checks.question: The painting was made in about 1662–63 for the VOC. What can it show us?

options.text: What happened to Bandanese people in 1621
options.feedback: Not quite. The painting was made more than 40 years later. It shows no one who was harmed.

options.text: What every Bandanese person thought of the VOC
options.feedback: Not quite. The VOC paid for the painting. Look at who made it in the third part.

options.text: How the company chose to show Banda
options.feedback: Yes. It shows the company's perspective: forts, a ship and neat rows of trees.

checks.question: Coen wrote that almost nobody escaped. Why might a leader write something that was not true?

visual.description: PLACEHOLDER: not drawn yet. An original Thinkerwell diagram in two panels side by side, with the label "trade connections, schematic" in one corner. Left panel, headed "Before: many buyers": a small cluster of islands in the centre labelled "Banda Islands: nutmeg and mace", with four thin solid two-way arrows to four plain boxes labelled "Indonesia", "China and India", "Persia and Arabia" and "later: Portugal, the Netherlands, England". The arrows show who traded, not routes: no coastline, no ships, no exact paths. Right panel, headed "After: VOC demands exclusive control": the same islands with a small fort symbol, one thick one-way arrow to a box "VOC: the only buyer", and the other four boxes greyed out behind a short bar labelled "shut out". Under the fort, a small label "taken by force, 1621". No people, faces, flags, weapons or violence drawn. Words carry every meaning; colour is never the only clue.
visual.alt: Two diagrams side by side. Before: the Banda Islands trade nutmeg and mace with several groups of traders, shown by two-way arrows. After: the VOC is the only buyer, the other traders are shut out, and a fort on the islands is labelled “taken by force, 1621”.
visual.caption: A Thinkerwell diagram of what a monopoly changed. The arrows show who could trade. They are not real sea routes.
visual.lookClosely: How does an exclusive rule change who may choose a buyer?

secondVisual.description: Wikimedia Commons file "Gezicht op Banda, zuidelijke Molukken Rijksmuseum SK-A-4476.jpeg": a photograph of the oil painting View of Banda Neira (Rijksmuseum SK-A-4476), about 1662–63, attributed to the workshop of Johannes Vingboons and commissioned by the VOC's Amsterdam chamber. It is a bird's-eye view of the island labelled "NEYRA", with a Dutch ship off a walled fort, a star-shaped fort on higher ground, a red-roofed village and fenced rows of nutmeg trees. Chosen because it is a dated company source made decades after 1621, which lets learners ask what a commissioned picture shows and whose experience it leaves out.
secondVisual.alt: A painted view from above of a long, flat island labelled NEYRA. A large sailing ship with a Dutch flag lies off a low walled fort. Behind it a star-shaped fort stands on higher ground, with red-roofed buildings to the left and long rows of trees to the right. No people can be seen clearly.
secondVisual.caption: A painting of Banda Neira, made for the VOC in about 1662–63. That is long after 1621. It shows what the company wanted to show. It cannot tell us what Bandanese people lived through.
secondVisual.lookClosely: What is prominent? Whose viewpoint is absent?

sensitiveNotes: This lesson covers the VOC's conquest of Banda in 1621: mass killing, enslavement and forced removal. The Dutch National Archives' teaching page is titled “Genocide op Banda (1621)”. Learner text states it plainly, once, with no detail and no death toll; sources give different numbers (the archives: up to 15,000 people before, about 1,000 left on the islands; the Rijksmuseum: all 15,000 killed or driven away), so never ask learners to learn a figure. Some learners may have lived through violence or forced displacement: say before part 2 what it covers, let anyone read the simpler text or step away, and never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, displacement, their country, religion or ethnicity. Don't present the events as a disagreement with two equal sides, and never invent a Bandanese first-person quotation. The TED-Ed video describes the violence in far more detail than the lesson (see its note): preview it first.
educatorNotes: Aim: learners name the VOC's monopoly and the harm it brought, and say whose account a company source leaves out. Evidence move (brief 3B): read Coen's report as a company source (he led the attack, and the archives show his claim that almost nobody escaped was false: about 1,700 Bandanese escaped), then look at the later commissioned painting. A sound answer names the monopoly and the harm and identifies a missing account. Misconception to catch: a fort or an orderly ship in the painting does not prove trade was voluntary or that the VOC caused no harm. Banda's history did not end in 1621: people who escaped kept it alive, for example in the Kei Islands, through songs and dances such as the Wanar dance (Dutch National Archives).

Source caveats: the Dutch National Archives says its collection holds no sources with Bandanese voices, so every archive source on Banda tells the story from a colonial view. Its page shows Coen's 6 May 1621 report on the decision to starve out Banda Besar; the lesson describes it only in general terms and never quotes it. The Rijksmuseum says the painting was commissioned by the VOC's Amsterdam chamber from the Vingboons workshop before 30 April 1663, probably for the directors' meeting room, and was based on company maps: Neira never had five nutmeg gardens, and the hills behind are imagined. Before the VOC, the Westfries Museum says Dutch traders at first paid port fees and bought spice like other visitors, which helps show the change from trade to force.
changes: Written on 1 November 2026 from Justin's course brief (28 October 2026), sections 3 and 3A.

Facts checked against the Dutch National Archives' teaching page (in Dutch), the Westfries Museum's PALA article and the Rijksmuseum record, all opened on 1 November 2026. 3A's list of traders (England, Portugal, the Netherlands) is widened to the archives' list: traders from Indonesia, China, India, Persia and Arabia came first. 3A's “built a fort without the agreement of everyone” is now “began to build a fort; the people there refused the company's demands”, as the archives put it.

Added two points from the archives that the brief's evidence move needs: Coen claimed almost nobody escaped, which was false, and some Bandanese escaped and kept Banda's history in songs and dances. Added one sentence that enslaved people were then forced to grow the nutmeg, so learners can ask who worked in the painting's gardens. Did not use the word genocide in learner text, though the archives do (see sensitiveNotes).

3A calls Source A “a letter Coen sent to the VOC directors”. The archives' page captions it “Coen's report on the decision to starve out [Banda Besar], 6 May 1621” and does not say who received it, so the lesson calls it a report. A reviewer could confirm the recipient in VOC archive 1.04.02, inventory 1073.

Commons file checked on 1 November 2026: Artwork by Johannes Vingboons (“attributed to”), between 1662 and 1663, Rijksmuseum SK-A-4476, public domain (PD-old, PD-US) and CC0 from the Rijksmuseum, as the brief says. The Rijksmuseum's own record now says “workshop of Johannes Vingboons” and confirms the VOC commission; the credit follows the museum.
The warnings for “kill” in learner text are deliberate: the brief asks for the 1621 events to be stated plainly.

Watch left out (1 November 2026): TED-Ed's video by the historian Adam Clulow on the Banda Islands (OxeTFB84e2k, 4:47) fits the lesson, but by TED's own transcript its narration describes torture, starvation, people jumping from cliffs and an official calling for the Bandanese to be "entirely exterminated": too graphic for refugee learners aged 12–15 without a person watching it first. The lesson has four steps until someone watches it and decides; its written summary from the transcript is in git history.
